summary.text: Axial tilt, or obliquity, is the angle between a body's spin axis and the line standing at right angles to the plane of its orbit.
Earth's axis keeps pointing the same way all year, so each hemisphere leans toward the Sun for half the orbit and away for the other half, which causes the seasons.
Earth's tilt, now about 23.44°, has swung between roughly 22° and 24.5° with a mean period of about 41,000 years, likely helping drive long-term climate change.

items.prompt: Picture a planet whose spin axis stands at exactly 0°, at right angles to its orbit. What would its seasons be like?

options.label: Extreme ones, with sunlight beating straight down on the poles
Twice as long as Earth's, since nothing slows them down
No pole would lean sunward, so no tilt-driven seasons
The same as Earth's, only reversed between hemispheres

items.explain: Seasons come from one pole leaning toward the Sun and then away; with zero tilt, neither pole leans either way.

items.prompt: It is midsummer in Canada. Which way is Earth's North Pole leaning?

options.label: Away from the Sun
Toward the Sun
Straight up, square to the Sun
Toward the Moon

items.explain: Northern Hemisphere summer happens when the North Pole is directed toward the Sun and the South Pole away.

items.prompt: Our large Moon has an important effect on how far Earth's axis leans. What is it?

options.label: It tips Earth a little further over every year
It makes the lean flip over every few thousand years
It has no measurable effect on the lean at all
It steadies the lean, keeping wild swings away

items.explain: The Moon has a stabilizing effect on Earth's obliquity; without it, some studies found the tilt could swing far more.

items.prompt: Many people think summer comes when Earth is nearer the Sun. What actually causes the seasons?

options.label: The slanted axis turning each hemisphere sunward, then away
Earth's distance from the Sun changing over the year
The Sun itself giving off more energy in some months
The Moon blocking some sunlight for part of the year

items.explain: Because the tilted axis keeps a fixed direction, each hemisphere faces toward the Sun for part of the orbit and away for the rest; that is the cause of the seasons.

items.prompt: Over the past 5 million years, about how long has Earth's lean taken, on average, to swing through one full cycle?

options.label: About 1 year
About 670 years
About 41,000 years
About 4 million years

items.explain: Earth's obliquity has varied between about 22° and 24.5° with a mean period of 41,040 years.

items.prompt: In December, Earth is on the opposite side of the Sun from where it was in June. Relative to the distant stars, where does its axis point now?

options.label: The opposite way from where it pointed in June
Directly at the Sun, wherever Earth happens to be
At a right angle to where it pointed in June
The same way it pointed back in June

items.explain: Earth's axis stays tilted in the same direction against the background stars all year, a property called axial parallelism.
